paper.what: Every order, fill and profit figure on this page was simulated against a recorded order book. Nothing was sent to an exchange.
paper.why: It is the whole posture of the system: the research runs for months before anyone decides whether to trade real money, and that decision is not made here.

fair value.what: Our estimate of the true probability, built from the prices sharp sportsbooks are quoting right now.
fair value.why: It is the number every simulated bet is measured against, so without it there is nothing to compare the market's price to.

staleness_s.what: How many seconds have passed since the fair price was last recomputed from a fresh sharp-book quote.
staleness_s.why: A fair price that is too old is a stale guess rather than a current one, and the strategy refuses to trade on it past a threshold.

CLV.what: Closing line value: whether the price we got was better than the price the market settled on right before kickoff.
CLV.why: It is the cleanest single measure of whether a bet was well-timed, independent of how the game itself turned out.

pinnacle_t5.what: The price Pinnacle, a sharp sportsbook, was quoting five minutes before the game started.
pinnacle_t5.why: It is one of the two closing benchmarks CLV is measured against, chosen because Pinnacle's line is widely treated as sharp.

consensus_close.what: The average closing price across the sharp books we track, rather than any single book's line.
consensus_close.why: It smooths out one book's quirks, giving a second, broader benchmark alongside pinnacle_t5.

kalshi_last_trade_pre_kick.what: The price of the last trade that actually printed on Kalshi before the game started.
kalshi_last_trade_pre_kick.why: It is a closing benchmark measured on Kalshi's own market rather than a sportsbook, so it reflects what Kalshi traders themselves believed.

result.what: How the game actually turned out, recorded after the fact.
result.why: Some scoring methods use the outcome directly and some deliberately do not, so naming it keeps a reader from confusing the two.

markout.plain: did the price move our way after the fill?
markout.what: Whether the market's price kept moving in our favor for a short window after our simulated order filled.
markout.why: It scores execution quality on its own, separate from whether the underlying bet itself eventually won.

intent.what: A record that the strategy wanted to place a bet at a certain price, made before any order existed.
intent.why: It is the starting point of the funnel: every skip and every simulated order traces back to one of these.

skip.what: An intent the executor did not turn into a simulated order, along with the reason it was passed on.
skip.why: Skips are where most of the funnel's shrinkage happens, so naming the reason is what keeps the funnel honest.

queue_ahead_at_place.plain: orders ahead of ours when we placed
queue_ahead_at_place.what: How many contracts of resting size were in front of our simulated order at the moment it was placed.
queue_ahead_at_place.why: It sets the starting point for how much trading has to happen before our order could realistically fill.

queue_remaining.what: How many contracts are still in front of our simulated order right now, after accounting for trades since it was placed.
queue_remaining.why: Zero means our order would fill on the very next trade at that price, which is exactly what this number makes visible.

queue_model.plain: filled from the recorded order book
queue_model.what: A fill decided by replaying the recorded order book rather than by actually resting an order on an exchange.
queue_model.why: It is how every fill on this page is simulated, and it is why none of them is real money.

no_watcher.plain: would have filled without our watcher
no_watcher.what: A simulated fill that the queue model would have produced even if nothing had been watching the book at all.
no_watcher.why: It flags fills a naive queue estimate could get right by luck, so they are not overcounted as evidence the model works.

snapshot_cross.what: A moment when the recorded best price moved through our simulated order's price, rather than a trade printing exactly at it.
snapshot_cross.why: It is one of two ways a fill gets simulated, and it is the weaker one because no trade is known to have actually happened there.

has_print.plain: a real trade printed at our price
has_print.what: A moment when a trade is recorded in the tape at exactly our simulated order's price.
has_print.why: It is the stronger of the two fill signals, because a real trade at that price is direct evidence a fill was possible.

n_clusters.what: How many separate games the estimate rests on. Several bets on the same game count once.
n_clusters.why: Bets in the same game rise and fall together, so counting bets would make a handful of games look like a mountain of evidence.

honest range.what: A 90 percent confidence interval computed by clustering bets that share a game, not by treating every bet as independent.
honest range.why: Treating correlated bets as independent would understate uncertainty and make thin evidence look far more solid than it is.

variant.what: One configuration of the strategy: its own rules for which markets to trade and at what price.
variant.why: Every table on this page is broken out by variant, because two variants can behave very differently even on the same data.

gate variant.what: The single variant whose results are being measured against the go-live gate's criteria right now.
gate variant.why: The gate evaluates one variant at a time, and naming it stops a reader from assuming the verdict covers every variant.

primary.what: The variant whose rules were fixed and written down before any of this week's data was seen.
primary.why: Every other variant is compared against it, because a rule chosen after seeing the data proves nothing on its own.

kill switch.plain: the stop button: no new orders, cancel everything
kill switch.what: A single operator control that stops the executor from placing new simulated orders and cancels every order it already has open.
kill switch.why: It is one of the only two writes the dashboard keeps; everything else on these pages is read-only evidence.

order book.plain: the live list of everyone's orders on Kalshi
order book.what: The current list of resting buy and sell orders on a Kalshi market, at every price level.
order book.why: It is what a real fill would trade against, which is why the queue model replays a recording of it rather than guessing.

tape.what: The order book as it was recorded over time, kept so a fill can be simulated after the fact rather than in real time.
tape.why: It is the raw record every simulated fill is built from, and it is one of the tables the nightly backup deliberately excludes.

dashboard snapshot.plain: this page's data, computed N seconds ago
dashboard snapshot.what: A cached read of the database, computed on a schedule rather than on every page load.
dashboard snapshot.why: It keeps a page load fast and the database light, at the cost of the data being a little behind live.

provisional.what: A week whose numbers can still change, because bets from it are still settling.
provisional.why: It warns a reader not to treat this week's row the way they would treat a finished, closed-out week.

gate criteria.plain: the twelve tests for going live
gate criteria.what: The fixed set of tests a variant's paper results must pass before trading real money is even considered.
gate criteria.why: Passing every one of them is necessary, but it is a research threshold, not a decision to trade real money.
